```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}

rootFolder = "./"

if(!exists("dispLineGraph")){
  source(paste0(rootFolder, "lib/common_profile.R"), local = TRUE)
}

## latest results objects written by figure.Rmd (figure/<date>/output/)
rds_file <- sort(Sys.glob("figure/*/output/results_objects.rds"), decreasing = TRUE)[1]
res <- readRDS(rds_file)
list2env(res, envir = environment())

latest_folder <- function(path){
  f <- list.files(path, full.names = TRUE)
  f[length(f)]
}
interp_exp1 <- read.csv(paste0(latest_folder(paste0(rootFolder, "Exp1/data")), "/zero_frac_summary.csv"))
interp_exp2 <- read.csv(paste0(latest_folder(paste0(rootFolder, "Exp2/data")), "/zero_frac_summary.csv"))
pct <- function(x) round(x * 100, 1)
## inter-sequence interval of Exp2 (interval_summary_exp2 from figure.Rmd)
iti <- function(a, col, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), interval_summary_exp2[interval_summary_exp2$analysis == a, col])
## "= 0.012" / "< 0.001" (round() alone prints p < .0005 as 0)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(round(p, 3) == 0, "< 0.001", paste0("= ", round(p, 3)))
## likelihood-ratio test as "$\chi^2$(df) = x, $p$ = y"
fmt_lrt <- function(chisq, df, p) paste0("$\\chi^2$(", df, ") = ", round(chisq, 3), ", $p$ ", fmt_p(p))
## maximal random-effects check of the pupil-bin models (figure.Rmd)
if(!exists("pupil_bin_maximal_exp1") || !exists("interval_summary_exp2")){
  stop("results_objects.rds is outdated (no pupil_bin_maximal_exp1 / interval_summary_exp2): knit figure.Rmd again first")
}
mx <- function(tab, g, what){
  r <- tab[tab$group == g,]
  switch(what,
         ri  = fmt_lrt(r$ri_chisq, 1, r$ri_p),
         max = fmt_lrt(r$max_chisq, 1, r$max_p),
         var = fmt_lrt(r$slope_var_chisq, r$slope_var_df, r$slope_var_p))
}

## AIC/BIC of the intercept-only, linear and U-shaped pupil-bin models
ic <- function(cmp, g){
  m <- cmp$models[cmp$models$group == g, ]
  v <- function(k, w) round(m[m$model == k, w], 3)
  paste0("intercept-only: AIC = ", v("null","AIC"), ", BIC = ", v("null","BIC"),
         "; linear: AIC = ", v("linear","AIC"), ", BIC = ", v("linear","BIC"),
         "; U-shaped: AIC = ", v("u_only","AIC"), ", BIC = ", v("u_only","BIC"))
}
## U-shaped vs intercept-only model
ut <- function(cmp, g){
  r <- cmp$tests[cmp$tests$group == g, ]
  paste0("$\\chi^2$(1) = ", round(r$u_chisq, 3), ", $p$ = ", round(r$u_p, 3), ", partial $r$ = ", round(r$u_partial_r, 3))
}
## time-bin LMM of Fig. 3B / Sup. Fig. 2A
wv <- function(tab, x, s){
  r <- tab[tab$x_position == x & tab$session == s, ]
  d <- sub(", \\$p\\$ = [^,]*$", "", r$descrip)
  d <- sub("\\) = 1$", ") = 1.000", d)
  paste0(d, ", $p_{FDR}$ ", fmt_p(r$p_fdr))
}
## fixed effect of an lmerTest coefficient table
cf <- function(tab, term) paste0("$b$ = ", round(tab[term,"Estimate"],3), ", $SE$ = ", round(tab[term,"Std. Error"],3),
                                 ", $t$(", round(tab[term,"df"],1), ") = ", round(tab[term,"t value"],3), ", $p$ = ", round(tab[term,"Pr(>|t|)"],3))
```

## Materials and methods
### Participants
A total of `r sum(df_sub$numOfSub)` participants (`r sum(df_sub$numOfMen)` men and `r sum(df_sub$numOfWomen)` women, aged `r min(c(dat_exp1$age,dat_exp2$age))`–`r max(c(dat_exp1$age,dat_exp2$age))` years, mean age = `r round(mean(c(dat_exp1$age,dat_exp2$age)),2)` years, SD = `r round(sd(c(dat_exp1$age,dat_exp2$age)),2)`), with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, took part in the experiments. `r df_sub[df_sub$exp==1,'numOfSub']` were completed to Experiment 1, and the remaining `r df_sub[df_sub$exp==2,'numOfSub']` to Experiment 2. In both experiments, the following exclusion criteria were applied to exclude participants who did not perform the task properly, based on their behavioral data. Participants were excluded as outliers since their T1 and T2 detection accuracy or false alarm (FA) rate exceeded a robust outlier criterion. Specifically, we first computed the median of T1, T2 detection accuracy and FA across participants. When the median was 1.0 (i.e., ceiling effects), we applied a z-score criterion based on the mean and standard deviation and excluded participants with $∣z∣$>3. Otherwise, we used the modified z-score based on the median absolute deviation (MAD) and excluded participants with $∣Mz∣$>3.5 (Iglewicz and Hoaglin, 1993). Two participants in Experiment 1 and five in Experiment 2 were excluded as outliers, resulting in final sample sizes of 18 and 26 participants, respectively.

Experiment 1 was conducted as an initial within-subject experiment to confirm the behavioral attentional blink effect and to explore whether spontaneous pupil dynamics were associated with trial-by-trial detection performance. The key observation from Experiment 1 was then tested more directly in Experiment 2, using an independent sample and a real-time pupil-triggered manipulation. Thus, Experiment 1 should be regarded as providing preliminary evidence that motivated the targeted validation in Experiment 2. The sample size for Experiment 2 was determined based on an a priori power analysis using G*Power for a repeated-measures within-subject design. Assuming a medium effect size of Cohen’s $f$ = 0.30 (partial η² = 0.083), an alpha level of 0.05, power of 0.80, two repeated measurements, a correlation among repeated measures of 0.50, and nonsphericity correction ε = 1, the analysis indicated that 24 participants were required. Given the assumed correlation, this effect size corresponds to a within-participant effect of $d_z$ ≈ `r sprintf("%.2f", 0.30 * sqrt(2 / (1 - 0.50)))` and was chosen following Cohen\'s (1988) guideline, in which $f$ = 0.30 lies between a medium and a large effect, providing a reasonable and conservative assumption (Cohen, 1998; Faul et al., 2009). We did not base the power analysis directly on these values because these corresponding time windows were identified post hoc from the time course observed in Experiment 1, and the estimates are therefore likely to be inflated.

All experimental procedures were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone (NTT) Communication Science Laboratories (R5-001) and were conducted in accordance with its ethical guidelines. All participants provided written informed consent.

### Pupil recording and preprocessing
The pupil data of both experiments were preprocessed offline with the same pipeline, which was based on the guidelines of (Kret and Sjak-Shie, 2019) with the modifications described below. Missing samples (blinks and tracking losses) and samples whose speed exceeded the median plus $n$ times the median absolute deviation (MAD) of the speed distribution were removed, with $n$ = 16. As recommended by Kret and Sjak-Shie (2019), the filter parameters were chosen empirically for our dataset. The speed threshold was derived from the participant’s speed distribution pooled across all runs, so that the same criterion was applied to all runs of a participant. Gaps of at least 75 ms were extended by 50 ms on each side to remove the unstable periods at the onset and offset of blinks. In addition, because a fixed 50-ms margin left residual post-blink dips in our data, each gap was further extended while the pupil signal still changed faster than 1.5 mm/s, by up to 100 ms before and 300 ms after the gap. Gaps separated by less than 100 ms were merged and stretches of valid data shorter than 100 ms between gaps were removed. The removed samples were interpolated with shape-preserving piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation (PCHIP). The preprocessed signal was then resampled to 200 Hz. For the participants included in the final analyses, the proportion of interpolated samples was `r pct(interp_exp1$interp_frac_mean)`% (SD = `r pct(interp_exp1$interp_frac_std)`%) in Experiment 1 (n = `r interp_exp1$n_sub`) and `r pct(interp_exp2$interp_frac_mean)`% (SD = `r pct(interp_exp2$interp_frac_std)`%) in Experiment 2 (n = `r interp_exp2$n_sub`).

### Linear mixed-effects models
Nested models were fitted with maximum likelihood and compared with likelihood-ratio tests using the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015); $p$ values of individual fixed effects were obtained with the lmerTest package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017). The random-effects structure of each model was as follows. (i) Baseline pupil-size bins (Experiments 1 and 2): accuracy averaged within each participant and pupil-size bin was modeled with random intercepts for participants ($y \sim pupil\ bin + (1|subject)$). (ii) Time bins relative to pupil dilation and constriction phase (Experiment 1): single-trial accuracy was modeled with random intercepts for participants ($y \sim 1 + (1|subject)$). The intercept estimated the deviation of accuracy in that bin from the overall accuracy and was tested against zero, that is, compared with the overall accuracy. Because this test concerns the mean deviation across participants, the degrees of freedom were obtained with the Kenward-Roger approximation. (iii) Phase condition with baseline pupil size as a covariate (Experiment 2): accuracy averaged within each participant, lag, and phase condition was modeled with random intercepts and by-participant random slopes for phase condition ($y \sim lag + phase + baseline\ pupil + (1 + phase|subject)$). We also fitted the maximal models with by-participant random slopes for (i) to (iii), and their results are reported in the Supplementary Material.

# Results
## Experiment 1
### Behavioral data
We first confirmed that participants could detect the T1 and T2 in T1- and T2-only sequences, respectively, as well as T1 in the T1T2 sequence. Accuracies for T1 and the probe (T2) were consistently high, indicating that participants were able to reliably discriminate the target sounds from the distractors (T1: M=`r round(mean(df_accuracy_T1$hit_t1),3)`, SD=`r round(sd(df_accuracy_T1$hit_t1),3)`, Probe: M=`r round(mean(df_accuracy_T2$hit_t2),3)`, SD=`r round(sd(df_accuracy_T2$hit_t2),3)`; see Figure 1B and 1C). We then examined whether the auditory stimuli elicited an attentional blink, as reflected in reduced T2 detection when participants attended to both T1 and T2 relative to when they ignored T1. To test this, we compared T2 detection accuracy across lag conditions between the T1-attend and T1-ignore conditions using a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with lag and session (T1-attend vs. T1-ignore) as within-subject factors. The analysis revealed a significant main effect of session (`r showAnovaSummary(PT1T2_anova,bf_table,4,2)`). Post hoc analyses showed that, consistent with previous studies, probe detection probability significantly decreased in the T1-attend condition compared to the T1-ignore condition (ps < .05), except at lag 2 (p = `r round(PT1T2_anova_post[["A:B"]][["simtab"]][7,"p.col"],3)`) as shown in Figure 1D. We also observed a significant main effect of lag (`r showAnovaSummary(PT1T2_anova,bf_table,2,1)`), whereas the interaction between lag and session was not significant (`r showAnovaSummary(PT1T2_anova,bf_table,6,3)`).

### Relationship between baseline pupil size and T2|T1 detection accuracy
We hypothesized that baseline pupil size would be associated with T2|T1 detection accuracy, given that previous studies have linked baseline pupil size to perceptual performance (McGinley et al., 2015; Kempen et al., 2019; Beerendonk et al., 2024; Gee et al., 2024). To test this hypothesis, we compared pupil diameter during the 1-s period preceding T1 onset between hit and miss trials in the T1-attend and T1-ignore conditions. Pupil time courses around target presentation are shown in Figure 2A. The same time courses aligned to T2 onset and baseline-corrected pupil responses aligned to T1 onset are shown in Supplementary Figure 1. Baseline pupil size was defined as the mean pupil diameter during the 1-s period immediately preceding the onset of each auditory sequence, thereby avoiding potential contamination from target- and distractor-evoked pupil responses. The baseline pupil size was averaged across lag conditions and separated by response (hit vs. miss), as shown in Figure 2B. The results showed that baseline pupil size was significantly smaller for hit trials compared to miss trials although the Bayes factor did not provide evidence for this main effect (`r showAnovaSummary(anova_BP,bf_table_BP,4,2)`). Despite the non-significant interaction (`r showAnovaSummary(anova_BP,bf_table_BP,6,3)`), exploratory follow-up comparisons showed that this effect was present only in the T1-attend condition (`r showTtestSummary(ttest_BP[["T1-attend"]])`), but not in the T1-ignore condition (`r showTtestSummary(ttest_BP[["T1-ignore"]])`).

To further characterize this relationship between the range of baseline pupil sizes and detection performance, trials were sorted according to baseline pupil size and divided into five bins from smallest to largest following Kempen et al (2019). Accuracy for each bin was plotted separately for each attention condition (Figure 2C). Following the paper, detection accuracy was first averaged within each subject and pupil-size bin, separately for each attention condition. We then compared two nested linear mixed-effects models fitted with maximum likelihood of an intercept-only model ($y \sim 1 + (1|subject)$) and a model including a linear pupil-bin term ($y \sim pupil\ bin + (1|subject)$). The significance of the pupil-bin effect was assessed using a likelihood-ratio test comparing these two models. The linear pupil-bin term showed a negative relationship with probe detection probability in the T1-attend condition (`r showEstimateSummary(estimateAll[1,])`), indicating that detection probability increased as baseline pupil size decreased. This pupil-bin relationship was not observed in the T1-ignore condition (`r showEstimateSummary(estimateAll[2,])`).

To examine whether a nonlinear relationship better accounted for the data, we additionally compared three mixed-effects models using AIC and BIC: an intercept-only model, a linear pupil-bin model, and a U-shaped model including only the quadratic pupil-bin term. In the T1-attend condition, both AIC and BIC selected the linear model over the U-shaped model (`r ic(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp1, "T1-attend")`). In the T1-ignore condition, BIC selected the intercept-only model, whereas AIC slightly favored the U-shaped model (`r ic(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp1, "T1-ignore")`). The U-shaped model did not improve the fit over the intercept-only model in either the T1-attend condition (`r ut(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp1, "T1-attend")`) or the T1-ignore condition (`r ut(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp1, "T1-ignore")`). Thus, Experiment 1 did not provide evidence that a U-shaped model better explained the relationship between baseline pupil size and detection accuracy.

### Relationship between slow pupil change and T2|T1 detection accuracy
We next tested the hypothesis that T2|T1 detection accuracy varies systematically across the phase of spontaneous slow pupil fluctuations. To test this, we examined low-frequency pupil dynamics by applying a 0.15-Hz low-pass filter to the pupil signal, given that these fluctuations have been linked to ongoing changes in brain state and sensory processing. To characterize these slow dynamics, we identified pupil troughs and peaks, which marked the onset of the pupil-dilation (PD) and pupil-constriction (PC) phases, respectively. Figure 3A illustrates an example where pupil constriction events were indicated by blue markers and Figure 3B (upper panel) shows the PD phase following the PC phase. Pupil dynamics following the PC phase are shown in Supplementary Figure 2A. For each trial, we calculated the interval between the most recent pupil event and T1 onset and assigned the trial to one of six consecutive 1-s bins following the event. We then calculated T2|T1 detection accuracy within each bin and expressed it as the deviation from the overall mean accuracy. The deviation of bin-wise T2|T1 detection accuracy from the overall accuracy in the PD phase is shown collapsed across lags (Figure 3B, lower panel) and separately for each lag (Figure 3C). For each attention condition and phase-onset type, a separate linear mixed-effects model was fitted to each time bin. The dependent variable was single-trial T2|T1 accuracy, from which the effect of run was regressed out and the mean of each participant, attention condition, and lag was subtracted. The model included a fixed intercept and a random intercept for participant ($y \sim 1 + (1|subject)$), and the intercept was tested against zero. Because six-time bins were tested within each attention condition, we corrected for multiple comparisons by applying the Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) procedure separately within each condition’s six bins. The time-bin analyses suggested that the accuracy for P(T2|T1) improved immediately following the PD phase, an effect that was clearest during the 1–2s interval in the T1-attend condition (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_troughs, 2, "T1-attend")`), which remained significant after FDR correction. A similar but weaker trend was present during the 0–1s interval (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_troughs, 1, "T1-attend")`), whereas the 2–3s interval showed only a small, non-significant deviation (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_troughs, 3, "T1-attend")`) in the T1-attend condition. In contrast, accuracy in the later 4–5s interval in the T1-attend condition was significantly lower than the overall accuracy (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_troughs, 5, "T1-attend")`). In the T1-ignore condition, none of the six intervals showed a significant effect, including the 1–2s interval (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_troughs, 2, "T1-ignore")`). Following the PC phase, the pattern was reversed in the T1-attend condition (Supplementary Figure 2A). Accuracy was significantly lower than the overall accuracy during the 0–1 s (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_peaks, 1, "T1-attend")`) and 1–2 s intervals (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_peaks, 2, "T1-attend")`), and the 4–5 s interval showed a non-significant positive trend (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_peaks, 5, "T1-attend")`). In the T1-ignore condition, no interval survived FDR correction, including the 0–1 s (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_peaks, 1, "T1-ignore")`) and 1–2 s intervals (`r wv(annotation_df_wave_peaks, 2, "T1-ignore")`). For reference, the results of the same analysis with other cutoff frequencies (`r length(unique(cutoff_sweep_exp1$cutoff_hz))` cutoffs from `r min(cutoff_sweep_exp1$cutoff_hz)` to `r max(cutoff_sweep_exp1$cutoff_hz)` Hz) are provided in Supplementary Figure 3.

## Experiment 2
### Behavioral data
To validate the improvement in AB detection following the PD phase observed in Experiment 1, we implemented real-time pupil monitoring and presented T1 at specific phases of slow pupil fluctuations (<0.15 Hz), corresponding to the PD or PC phase. Figure 4A shows pupil dynamics immediately preceding T1 presentation in both conditions. As intended, T1 was successfully presented within 0–1 s after the onset of the PD or PC phase (Supplementary Figure 4A). Because each sound sequence was triggered by the real-time pupil criterion rather than at fixed intervals, the interval between successive sequence onsets varied (Supplementary Figure 4B). The mean inter-sequence interval, averaged across participants, was `r iti("LBP","mean")` s in the PC phase (SD across participants = `r iti("LBP","sd")` s; mean within-participant SD = `r iti("LBP","within_sd")` s; range = `r iti("LBP","min",1)`–`r iti("LBP","max",1)` s) and `r iti("SBP","mean")` s in the PD phase (SD across participants = `r iti("SBP","sd")` s; mean within-participant SD = `r iti("SBP","within_sd")` s; range = `r iti("SBP","min",1)`–`r iti("SBP","max",1)` s). Detection accuracy for the T1- and T2-only sequences remained high (T1: M=`r round(mean(df_accuracy_T1_exp2$hit_t1),3)`, SD=`r round(sd(df_accuracy_T1_exp2$hit_t1),3)`, Probe: M=`r round(mean(df_accuracy_T2_exp2$hit_t2),3)`, SD=`r round(sd(df_accuracy_T2_exp2$hit_t2),3)`; see Supplementary Figures 5A and 5B). We confirmed that mean pupil size around T1 onset did not significantly differ between the PD and PC phases as shown in Figure 4B (`r showTtestSummary(anovaTable$ttest_pupil_size_exp2)`) .

### Relationship between baseline pupil size and T2|T1 detection accuracy in Experiment 2
To examine whether the relationship between baseline pupil size and detection performance observed in Experiment 1 could be replicated under real-time pupil-triggered presentation, we repeated the same bin-based analysis in Experiment 2 (see Supplementary Figure 5C). Trials were sorted according to baseline pupil size and divided into five bins from smallest to largest, following the same procedure as in Experiment 1. Detection accuracy for P(T2|T1) was then calculated separately for each bin and phase condition. Consistent with the results of Experiment 1, probe detection probability decreased as baseline pupil size increased in the PC phase (`r showEstimateSummary(estimateAll_exp2[estimateAll_exp2$analysis=="LBP",])`) but not in the PD phase (`r showEstimateSummary(estimateAll_exp2[estimateAll_exp2$analysis=="SBP",])`) as Supplementary Figure 5C. However, the slope of this relationship varied considerably across participants. The between-participant SD of the slope (`r round(pupil_bin_maximal_exp2[pupil_bin_maximal_exp2$group=="LBP","slope_sd"],3)` in the PC phase) was larger than the absolute value of the mean slope (`r round(estimateAll_exp2[estimateAll_exp2$analysis=="LBP","Estimate"],3)`), and including by-participant random slopes for pupil bin improved the model fit (PC phase: `r mx(pupil_bin_maximal_exp2, "LBP", "var")`; PD phase: `r mx(pupil_bin_maximal_exp2, "SBP", "var")`). When these random slopes were included (see “Linear mixed-effects models”), the pupil-bin effect was `r ifelse(pupil_bin_maximal_exp2[pupil_bin_maximal_exp2$group=="LBP","max_p"] < 0.05, "still significant", "no longer significant")` in the PC phase (`r mx(pupil_bin_maximal_exp2, "LBP", "max")`) and `r ifelse(pupil_bin_maximal_exp2[pupil_bin_maximal_exp2$group=="SBP","max_p"] < 0.05, "significant", "not significant")` in the PD phase (`r mx(pupil_bin_maximal_exp2, "SBP", "max")`).

We again compared the linear model with the U-shaped model using AIC and BIC. In the PC phase, both AIC and BIC selected the linear model over the U-shaped model (`r ic(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp2, "LBP")`), and the U-shaped model did not significantly improve the fit over the intercept-only model (`r ut(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp2, "LBP")`). In the PD phase, AIC selected the linear model and BIC selected the intercept-only model (`r ic(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp2, "SBP")`), and the U-shaped model did not improve the fit over the intercept-only model (`r ut(pupil_bin_model_comparison_exp2, "SBP")`). Thus, these model comparisons did not support replacing the linear model with a U-shaped model.

Taken together, in Experiment 2, smaller baseline pupil size was associated with higher T2|T1 detection accuracy on average, in the same direction as in Experiment 1. However, this relationship was not consistent across participants and therefore cannot be regarded as a robust effect.

### PD-phase triggering improved T2|T1 detection relative to PC-phase triggering
Our primary hypothesis was that triggering target presentation during the PD phase would improve T2|T1 detection relative to triggering during the PC phase. To assess this hypothesis, we compared lag-dependent T2|T1 detection accuracy between the two-phase conditions using a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA examining the main effect of phase condition. Accuracy in the PD phase was significantly higher than in the PC phase (`r showAnovaSummary(anova_BP_exp2,bf_table_exp2,4,2)`), consistent with our prediction based on the phase-triggering manipulation. The participant-wise differences in P(T2|T1) between the PD and PC phases are shown in Supplementary Figure 6A. To determine whether pupil phase also shifted the temporal extent of the attentional blink, we estimated the lag threshold (50% of accuracy, corresponding to the conventional midpoint of the psychometric function (Wichmann and Hill, 2001) from the fitted psychometric functions for each phase condition and assessed its uncertainty via parametric bootstrap (10,000 iterations). Figure 4C shows lag-dependent P(T2|T1) performance. Supplementary Figure 6B shows the bootstrap distributions of the threshold estimates for each condition. The 95% bootstrap confidence interval for the threshold difference between the PC and PD phases (PC – PD) was [`r round(quantile(diffs,0.025),3)`, `r round(quantile(diffs,0.975),3)`], indicating that the threshold was significantly higher in the PC phase than in the PD phase.

As described in the preceding section, baseline pupil size showed a negative association with detection performance in the random-intercept model in Experiment 2. We therefore tested whether the improved detection performance during the PD phase could be explained merely by differences in baseline pupil size. To rule out this possibility, we fitted linear mixed-effects models with lag condition, phase condition, and baseline pupil size as fixed effects, and subject-specific random intercepts and phase slopes to explain detection accuracy. We compared this model with a model that included lag condition and phase condition but not baseline pupil size. In the model without baseline pupil size, accuracy was higher in the PD phase than in the PC phase (`r cf(phase_covariate_exp2$coefficients_phase_only, "analysisSBP")`). Adding baseline pupil size did not improve the model fit ($\chi^2$(`r phase_covariate_exp2$baseline_test$df`) = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$baseline_test$chisq,3)`, $p$ = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$baseline_test$p,3)`), and both AIC and BIC favored the model without baseline pupil size (without baseline pupil size: AIC = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$phase_only_vs_baseline$AIC[1],3)`, BIC = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$phase_only_vs_baseline$BIC[1],3)`, with baseline pupil size: AIC = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$phase_only_vs_baseline$AIC[2],3)`, BIC = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$phase_only_vs_baseline$BIC[2],3)`). In the model with baseline pupil size, the effect of phase condition was nearly unchanged and remained significant (`r cf(phase_covariate_exp2$coefficients, "analysisSBP")`), whereas baseline pupil size itself was not significant (`r cf(phase_covariate_exp2$coefficients, "PD")`). Adding the lag-by-phase interaction to this model did not improve model fit ($\chi^2$(`r phase_covariate_exp2$interaction_test$df`) = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$interaction_test$chisq,3)`, $p$ = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$interaction_test$p,3)`, AIC = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$model_comparison$AIC[3],3)`, BIC = `r round(phase_covariate_exp2$model_comparison$BIC[3],3)`). This result indicates that the phase-related difference in T2|T1 accuracy cannot be explained solely by baseline pupil size.
